'''Thomas W. Mossberg''' (born 1951) is an American physicist, formerly of [[Columbia University|Columbia]], [[Harvard University|Harvard]], and the [[University of Oregon]]. He was also the founding President and CEO at LightSmyth Technologies, a [[nanotechnology]] company in [[Eugene, Oregon]].

== Early life and education ==
The son of William and Rosemary (née Kotilinek) Mossberg, Thomas William Mossberg was born in 1951 in [[Hennepin County, Minnesota|Hennepin, Minnesota]].<ref>{{Cite web |year=1951 |title=Minnesota Birth Index |url=https://www.ancestry.com/discoveryui-content/view/9265830:8742 |url-access=subscription |access-date=2022-06-11 |website=www.ancestry.com}}</ref> He completed his undergraduate work at the [[University of Chicago]] in 1973. He earned a Ph.D. at [[Columbia University]] 1978, with a dissertation titled, ''Excited-state, tri-level, and two-photon echoes in atomic sodium vapor,''<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mossberg |first=Thomas William |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NODkXasJrKkC&dq=%22Excited-state,+tri-level,+and+two-photon+echoes+in+atomic+sodium+vapor%22&pg=RA2-PA115 |title=Excited-state, tri-level, and two-photon echoes in atomic sodium vapor. |publisher=NASA, Office of Scientific and Technical Information |year=1978 |pages=115 |language=en}}</ref> advised by Sven R. Hartmann.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Physics Tree - Thomas William Mossberg Family Tree |url=https://academictree.org/physics/tree.php?pid=187711 |access-date=June 11, 2022|website=academictree.org}}</ref>

== Career ==
After faculty positions at Columbia University and [[Harvard University]], Mossberg joined the physics faculty at the [[University of Oregon]] from 1986–1999.<ref>{{Cite news |date=September 21, 2005 |title=Former physics professor sues UO |pages=9 |work=Corvallis Gazette-Times |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/103495744/former-physics-professor-sues-uo/ |access-date=June 11, 2022}}</ref> Colleague Michael Raymer wrote, "Thomas Mossberg (Ph.D. Columbia Univ., 1978) in 1987 established a group to study experimental [[quantum optics]]. His group was first to demonstrate narrowing below the [[Spectral line|natural line width]] of an atomic emission line by the modification of the density of optical states within an [[optical cavity]]. In 1999 Mossberg went on to found successful optical technology companies in the Eugene area."<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Raymer |first=Michael |date=March 20, 2016 |editor-last=Csonka |editor-first=Paul |title=Short historical summary of the UO Physics department, Optical Sciences |url=https://cpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/blogs.uoregon.edu/dist/0/5172/files/2016/10/PhysHist2016-1lpjqx1.pdf}}</ref>

In 1996, the [[American Physical Society]] reported on "recent advances in spectral holographic optical data storage" of Mossberg's research, leading to "high capacity, high speed, optical RAM, and content-controlled optical switching devices".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Data Storage, New Laser Advances Featured at ILS-XII Meeting |url=http://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/199612/meeting.cfm |access-date=2022-06-13 |website=www.aps.org |language=en}}</ref> Mossberg's research between 1995–1997 was supported by [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] grants valued at $492,530.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NSF Award Search: Award # 9421069 - Experimental Quantum Optics |url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=9421069 |access-date=2022-06-13 |website=www.nsf.gov}}</ref>

At the urging of the University Technology Transfer Office, Mossberg started Templex Technology, Inc.:
{{Blockquote
| quote = In 1995, technologies developed by University of Oregon physicist Thomas Mossberg became the basis of a new company, Templex Technology, Inc. Since that time the company, which develops innovative, high-bandwidth optical communications, has  grown to about thirteen employees. It recently re-located to the Riverfront Research Park adjacent to the UO. The new facility will allow Templex staffing to nearly double in the next year or two. On September 27, 1999, Templex announced that Intel Corporation has invested an undisclosed amount in the company. Templex intends to use the investment to further its product development, develop strategic partnerships, build company infrastructure, and create market awareness.<ref name=":0" />}}

Mossberg's research produced hardware with record-breaking information density and speed:
{{Blockquote
| quote = Thomas Mossberg is developing a new kind of optical computer memory that far surpasses the capabilities of today's magnetic storage devices (e.g., hard drives). His experimental hardware handles vast amounts of digital information, storing it in a small crystal that can be accessed at lightning speeds. The hardware already holds a world's record for information density and access speed, storing the equivalent of 700 floppy disks of information in one square inch of memory material...
A high-tech start-up company, Templex, has recently formed in Eugene to turn Mossberg's basic research into products for market. Only a year old, Templex already employs four Ph.D. physicists and additional staff members.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=Spring 1997 |title=Smaller, Faster, Better |url=https://scholarsbank.uoregon.edu/xmlui/bitstream/handle/1794/462/Inquiry_Vol3No1.pdf.txt?sequence=3 |journal=INQUIRY - UO Research Journal, A Magazine Highlighting Research |volume=III |issue=1 |via=scholarsbank.uoregon.edu}}</ref>}}

Mossberg also founded LightSmyth Technologies, serving as its president and CEO from 2000 until his retirement in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web |title=dun & bradstreet |url=https://www.dnb.com/business-directory/company-profiles.lightsmyth_technologies_inc.d828bcb1f8d89c030d639b2d067cdeb7.html |access-date=June 11, 2022 |website=dnb.com}}</ref> The firm had three [[NASA]] research awards between 2005–2007, at a total value of $769,744.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SBIR/STTR Firm Details - LightSmyth Technologies {{!}} NASA SBIR & STTR Program Homepage |url=https://sbir.nasa.gov/firm/node/34787 |access-date=2022-06-13 |website=sbir.nasa.gov}}</ref>  LightSmyth Technologies produced high performance transmission gratings and other diffractive devices for the optical communications industry.  In 2014, LightSmyth Technologies was acquired by Finisar Corporation<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hardy |first=Stephen |date=September 5, 2014 |title=Finisar buys gratings provider LightSmyth Technologies |url=https://www.lightwaveonline.com/business/mergers-acquisitions/article/16664191/finisar-buys-gratings-provider-lightsmyth-technologies |access-date=2022-07-23 |website=lightwaveonline.com}}</ref> which was in turn acquired by II-VI Corporation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=II-VI Completes Finisar Acquisition |url=https://www.photonics.com/Articles/II-VI_Completes_Finisar_Acquisition/a65143 |access-date=2022-07-23 |website=www.photonics.com}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
* Mossberg was elected an Optical Society of America Fellow in 1993.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022 |title=Optica Fellows |url=https://www.optica.org/get_involved/awards_and_honors/fellow_members/fellows_search/?searchtext=Mossberg+&searchmode=anyword&filteryear=0&filtergender=0&filtercountry=0&filterregion=0&sortfilters=1; |website=Optica (formerly Optical Society of America)}}</ref>
* In 1995, Mossberg was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]], cited ''For his work on optical resonance and cavity quantum electrodynamics, including the imaginative use of dressed-atom effects to control atomic dynamics and create new mechanisms for optical gain.''<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Fellow Archive |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1995&unit_id=DLS&institution=University+of+Oregon |access-date=June 1, 2022 |website=aps.org |language=en}}</ref>
